notes: \cpara{Reports a conversation. The author's remark that ``most organized belief systems exist to flee from doubt'' is reported, not argued. A listener answers that Jesuit novices are told to doubt their faith, and even to doubt that their doubts may grow stronger.}

\cpara{Says the report about the Jesuits could not be confirmed, and treats it as a possibly hypothetical case: if Jesuits did practice deliberate doubt, would that make them virtuous as rationalists? The hedge is kept in the next paragraph.}

\cpara{Concedes that such Jesuits would not be ``fleeing from doubt,'' but calls the conduct ``highly suspicious.'' To a truly virtuous rationalist doubt should not be scary, and the practice sounds like a program of getting used to something very scary.}

\clogic{This sits uneasily with the post's own closing rule, which grants that ``it may take courage to face your doubts'' and says that only ``to an ideal mind'' doubt would not be scary. For minds that are not ideal, practice in facing frightening doubts is what that rule would seem to call for.}
\cpara{Asks whether encouraging doubt is still worthwhile if the reasons for it are flawed.}
\cpara{Compares doubt to curiosity: each aims at its own end, which is an answer.}
\cpara{Claims that every doubt exists to destroy a particular belief or to die in the attempt, and that only the resolution of doubts moves rationality forward.}

\cpara{Restates the point: not every doubt is rational, and wearing doubts makes no one a rationalist, as a lab coat makes no one a doctor. The first sentence repeats, in reverse order, one from ``The Importance of Saying Oops,'' posted the day before.}

\cpara{The core of the post: a rational doubt has a specific reason, points to an investigation, and ends when the investigation ends. Two paragraphs later the post says that this ``is not widely understood.'' It is Charles Peirce's argument against Descartes's method of doubt, and Peirce is not mentioned. In 1868 Peirce wrote that someone who comes to doubt a belief ``doubts because he has a positive reason for it, and not on account of the Cartesian maxim. Let us not pretend to doubt in philosophy what we do not doubt in our hearts.'' In ``The Fixation of Belief'' (1877): ``There must be a real and living doubt, and without this all discussion is idle,'' and ``With the doubt, therefore, the struggle begins, and with the cessation of doubt it ends.''}

\clogic{Overstated, by the author's own earlier example. In ``The Proper Use of Humility'' (2006), the engineer who is ``damn sure'' a machine will not fail still builds fail-safes. That doubt is not resolved, and it changes the design. A doubt that investigation cannot settle can still rightly change what one does, as a hedge. The rule fits doubts that can be settled.}

\cpara{Asks why a real believer would give novices doubts that must die unfulfilled, comparing it to asking physics students to agonize over whether Newton was right after all. If you do not really doubt something, why pretend?}

\cpara{Answers with a claim about motives: ``we all want to be seen as rational,'' and people confuse doubt with modesty and status. No evidence is given for either claim. The earlier writing on humility is ``The Proper Use of Humility,'' which drew the same line between social modesty and the real thing.}
\cpara{Sums up the post in six rules. The footnote points to ``Professing and Cheering,'' earlier in the book.}
